extracted.subtask_description: Descriptions of practitioner roles in public relations and the skills, behaviors, and organizational conditions that lead to success (e.g., technician vs. manager roles, research use, diversity and ethics, and a short list of success traits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication Technician
rubrics_metrics.description: Entry-level practitioners hired to write and edit employee newsletters, write news releases and feature stories, develop website content, and deal with media contacts; typically not present when management defines problems and selects solutions and are brought in later to produce communication collateral and implement programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technicians focus on producing communications (press releases, speeches, websites, feature stories, annual reports). They often lack involvement in strategic planning, 'are the last to know,' and may experience lower pay and limited advancement compared with managers. This role constitutes the traditional core of PR work—writing mediated communications and doing media relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert Prescriber
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners seen as the authority on PR problems and solutions who define the problem, develop the program, and take full responsibility for implementation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful in crisis situations or when immediate action is needed, but long-term enactment can compartmentalize PR, exclude top management from decision making, create manager dependence on the practitioner, reduce managerial commitment to PR efforts, and lead to frustration and turnover as organizations search for someone to 'make problems go away.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication Facilitator
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners who act as sensitive listeners and information brokers—liaisons, interpreters, and mediators between an organization and its publics—maintaining two-way communication and keeping channels open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facilitators referee interactions, establish discussion agendas, summarize and restate views, call for reactions, and help diagnose and correct barriers to communication; they occupy boundary-spanning roles and assume that effective two-way communication improves decision quality for both management and publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem-Solving Process Facilitator
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners who collaborate with other managers to define and solve problems and become part of the strategic planning team from the first question through final evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They apply a step-by-step management problem-solving process, involve line managers (who have power to make changes), and foster shared understanding, support, and resource commitment for program goals. They are invited into management teams after demonstrating skill in helping other managers avoid and solve problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manager versus Technician role distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Two predominant roles: public relations technician (focused on writing/production) and public relations manager (part of organizational management, focusing on outcomes/impact).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manager role calls for research skills, strategic thinking, environmental scanning, negotiation and coalition building, issues management, program evaluation, and management counseling. Research finds that PR excellence is predicted by the extent to which top PR executives enact the manager role rather than the technician role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research and Information Gathering
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners who use all types of research and information gathering are most likely to operate in management roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of scientific, informal, and mixed research approaches correlates with manager-role enactment. Practitioners must actively gather information useful in decision making before being invited to the management table; research volume (not simply years on the job) determines likelihood of joining management. However, moving into the manager role does not automatically ensure mastery of it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role selection influenced by organizational environment
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner’s dominant role is a function of the organization’s environment (threat level and amount of change).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communication technicians tend to work in stable, low-threat organizations; communication facilitators in turbulent but low-threat settings; problem-solving process facilitators and expert prescribers occur in threatening environments. Expert prescribers appear when immediate action is imperative; problem-solving facilitators are preferred when there is time for collaborative processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity, Multiculturalism, and Inclusion (Cultural Competence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations must build and maintain relationships with all racial and ethnic segments; practitioners should develop cultural competence beyond language ability and cultural know-how to include respect, sensitivity, and appreciation of diversity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultural competence requires research to understand organizational and public cultures and situational identity. Inclusiveness involves recognizing different groups, listening, and taking their input into account. Diverse teams help monitor and address issues more effectively due to varied perspectives. Trends: growth of Hispanic population, recognition of LGBT communities, mobile/digital technologies, immigration, and aging populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pigeon-holing and cultural interpretation pitfalls
rubrics_metrics.description: Pigeon-holing: restricting minority practitioners to minority clients or publics; cultural interpretation: expecting a practitioner to know everything about a cultural group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are anti-patterns; rather than expecting only minority practitioners to communicate with minority publics, all practitioners should develop cultural competence. Discrimination and pigeon-holing limit career opportunities and effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professionalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessing PR as a profession using criteria such as specialized skills, knowledge, and commitment to professional and ethical standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional status historically tied to specialized education and entry standards; today, professionalism in PR is demonstrated by adherence to codes of ethics and the behavior of individual practitioners, which affects public perception of the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical Conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must choose to behave ethically; codes of ethics and individual behavior are central to professional status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical choices reflect on individuals, employers, clients, and the PR profession as a whole. Upholding the highest ethical standards is essential to earning respect from clients, the media, and the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for Success: Results
rubrics_metrics.description: Reputation for getting results and being goal oriented is the single most important key to success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers and clients pay for results, not merely hard work or effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for Success: Conceptualizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to focus on the employer’s or client’s needs; being a 'quick study' who is a good listener and thorough note taker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong conceptualizers can rapidly understand client needs and craft appropriate strategies and messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for Success: Human Relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Team players who balance personal goals with organizational goals and who know how to deal with management, even when in disagreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good human relations help practitioners navigate internal politics and build support for PR initiatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for Success: Style
rubrics_metrics.description: Traits such as a 'can-do' attitude and constructive competitiveness; translating confidence into persuasive advocacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Style-related traits support persuasive advocacy and substantive PR contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for Success: Intangibles
rubrics_metrics.description: Charisma, presence, and moxie—hard-to-describe qualities that affect how other managers evaluate PR professionals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn from the boss; know what your boss expects and find ways to make their job easier. Intangibles influence advancement and perceptions of capability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential Skills and Traits (writing, business understanding, technology, resilience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers seek understanding of how the business works, computer/software and new media skills, being well read and informed on current events, ability to deal with frustration and stress, and the ability to improvise. Above all, ability to write is number one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear writing is emphasized as the highest-priority skill; other traits (business acumen, tech literacy, media awareness, stress tolerance, improvisation) are also important for success in PR.
